title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch, after running into Vronsky on his own steps, drove on, as he had intended, to the Italian opera. He sat through two acts and saw everyone he had wanted to see. On returning home, he carefully looked over the hat stand, and noticing that no military overcoat was there, he went, as usual, to his room. But, contrary to his habit, he did not go to bed; he paced his study until three in the morning. The feeling of furious anger with his wife — who would not observe the proprieties and keep the one condition he had set on her, not to receive her lover in her own home — gave him no peace. She had not complied with his demand, and he was bound to punish her and carry out his threat — obtain a divorce and take away his son. He knew all the difficulties tied to this course, but he had said he would do it, and now he had to follow through. Countess Lidia Ivanovna had hinted that this was the best way out of his position, and lately the obtaining of divorces had been brought to such perfection that Alexey Alexandrovitch saw a way of overcoming the procedural obstacles. Misfortunes never come singly, and the affairs of the reorganization of the native tribes, and the irrigation of the lands of Zaraisky province, had brought such official troubles down on Alexey Alexandrovitch that he had been in a state of continual extreme irritation for some time.

He didn't sleep at all that night, and his fury, growing in a sort of vast arithmetical progression, reached its peak by morning. He dressed in a hurry, and as if carrying a cup full of wrath, afraid of spilling any, afraid of losing along with his wrath the energy he needed for the interview with his wife, he went into her room the moment he heard she was up.

Anna, who thought she knew her husband so well, was amazed at his appearance when he came in. His brow was lowering, and his eyes stared darkly past her, avoiding her gaze; his mouth was tightly and contemptuously shut. In his walk, in his gestures, in the sound of his voice there was a determination and firmness his wife had never seen in him. He went into her room and, without greeting her, walked straight to her writing-table, took her keys, and opened a drawer.
"What do you want?" she cried.
"Your lover's letters," he said.

"They're not here," she said, shutting the drawer; but from the action he saw he had guessed right, and roughly shoving her hand away, he quickly snatched up a portfolio in which he knew she kept her most important papers. She tried to pull the portfolio away, but he pushed her back.

"Sit down! I have to speak to you," he said, putting the portfolio under his arm and squeezing it so tightly with his elbow that his shoulder lifted. Amazed and intimidated, she stared at him in silence.
"I told you I would not allow you to receive your lover in this house."
"I had to see him to...."
She broke off, unable to find a reason.
"I do not go into the details of why a woman wants to see her lover."
"I meant, I only...." she said, flushing hotly. His coarseness angered her and gave her courage. "Surely you must feel how easy it is for you to insult me?" she said.
"An honest man and an honest woman can be insulted, but to call a thief a thief is simply _la constatation d'un fait_."
"This cruelty is something new — I didn't know it in you."
"You call it cruelty for a husband to give his wife liberty, granting her the honorable protection of his name, simply on the condition of observing the proprieties: is that cruelty?"
"It's worse than cruel — it's base, if you want to know!" Anna cried, in a rush of hatred, and getting up, she started to walk away.

"No!" he shrieked, in his shrill voice, which pitched a note higher than usual, and his big hands clutched her arm so violently that red marks were left from the bracelet he was squeezing, and he forced her back into her seat.
"Base! If you want to use that word, what is base is to abandon husband and child for a lover while you eat your husband's bread!"

She bowed her head. She did not say what she had said to her lover the evening before — that _he_ was her husband, and her husband was superfluous; she didn't even think it. She felt the full justice of his words, and only said softly:
"You cannot describe my position as worse than I feel it to be myself; but what are you saying all this for?"

"What am I saying it for? what for?" he went on, just as angrily. "So that you may know that since you haven't carried out my wishes about observing outward decorum, I will take measures to put an end to this state of affairs."
"Soon, very soon, it will end on its own," she said; and again, at the thought of death near at hand and now desired, tears came into her eyes.
"It will end sooner than you and your lover have planned! If you must have the satisfaction of animal passion...."
"Alexey Alexandrovitch! I won't say it's not generous, but it isn't like a gentleman to strike someone who's down."
"Yes, you only think of yourself! But the sufferings of the man who was your husband don't interest you. You don't care that his whole life is ruined, that he is thuff... thuff...."

Alexey Alexandrovitch was speaking so quickly that he stammered, and was utterly unable to get out the word "suffering." In the end he pronounced it "thuffering." She wanted to laugh, and was immediately ashamed that anything could amuse her at such a moment. And for the first time, for an instant, she felt for him, put herself in his place, and was sorry for him. But what could she say or do? Her head sank and she sat in silence. He too was silent for a while, then began to speak in a frigid, less shrill voice, stressing random words that carried no special meaning.
"I came to tell you...." he said.

She glanced up at him. "No, it was my imagination," she thought, remembering the expression on his face when he stumbled over the word "suffering." "No; can a man with those dull eyes, with that self-satisfied complacency, feel anything?"
"I cannot change anything," she whispered.

"I have come to tell you that I am going tomorrow to Moscow, and will not return to this house again, and you will receive notice of what I decide through the lawyer into whose hands I am putting the business of getting a divorce. My son is going to my sister's," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, recalling with an effort what he had meant to say about his son.
"You're taking Seryozha to hurt me," she said, looking at him from under her brows. "You don't love him.... Leave Seryozha with me!"
"Yes, I have lost even my affection for my son, because he is connected with the revulsion I feel for you. Still, I'll take him. Good-bye!"
And he was leaving, but now she held him back.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch, leave Seryozha with me!" she whispered once more. "I have nothing else to say. Leave Seryozha until my... I shall soon be confined; leave him with me!"
Alexey Alexandrovitch flew into a rage, snatched his hand away from her, and left the room without a word.
